story: When World War I broke out in August 1914, Canadian veterinarian Lieutenant Harry Colebourn boarded a train to report for military duty. During a stop in White River, Ontario, he spotted a trapper with an orphaned black bear cub and bought her for twenty dollars. He named her Winnipeg, or Winnie for short. Winnie became the official mascot of the Canadian Army Veterinary Corps, sailing across the Atlantic and living among the troops at Salisbury Plain. When Colebourn was ordered to the front lines in France, he left Winnie for safekeeping at the London Zoo. The bear proved so remarkably gentle that keepers allowed visitors inside her enclosure. Among her most devoted fans was a young boy named Christopher Robin Milne, who frequently visited the bear and renamed his own teddy bear in her honor, directly inspiring his father's timeless stories about Winnie-the-Pooh.
angle: The real Winnie-the-Pooh was a living World War I army mascot bought for $20 at a Canadian train stop by a cavalry vet.

claims.claim: Lieutenant Harry Colebourn purchased a black bear cub for $20 on August 24, 1914
The purchase took place during a train stop in White River, Ontario
Colebourn named the bear Winnipeg, shortened to Winnie, after his hometown in Manitoba
Winnie served as the mascot for the Canadian Army Veterinary Corps
Winnie sailed across the Atlantic aboard the S.S. Manitou in October 1914 with troops heading to England
Winnie lived with the troops at the military camp on Salisbury Plain
Colebourn left Winnie at the London Zoo on December 9, 1914, before heading to France
Colebourn ultimately chose to leave Winnie permanently at the zoo because she was loved and well cared for
A.A. Milne's son, Christopher Robin, frequently visited Winnie at the London Zoo starting in 1924
Christopher Robin renamed his own teddy bear from Edward Bear to Winnie-the-Pooh after the bear
Winnie died at the London Zoo in the year 1934

disputed: Whether the trapper's mother bear was killed in the spring of 1914 or shot specifically by that hunter; the script should note she was orphaned or leave out the exact details of the mother's fate.
Whether children fed Winnie honey or condensed milk; sources vary, so the script can mention feeding treats or attribute specific foods like condensed milk or honey to accounts.
